verdict: Avoid new hosiery and knitwear exposure in Ludhiana until raw-material costs and the credit-to-output gap correct; lend only to branded, export-diversified converters with tight monthly monitoring.
title: Ludhiana Hosiery & Knitwear: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Ludhiana spins, knits, dyes and stitches winterwear and innerwear, selling to wholesale markets across India and to exporters. **Cash turns on the dyeing and stitching cycle, not on the knitting machines** — value sits in the finished garment and in the buyer relationship, while the fixed assets are modest and largely reusable. The city is a major winterwear hub supplying markets across India [2].

## What has changed now
**Raw-material costs have risen about 40 per cent in recent months, squeezing converters who cannot pass it on** [2]. Nationally, IIP for NIC 14 (wearing apparel) is down 7.4% YoY and 5.6% Apr-to-date [D], and exports are down 6.2% Apr-to-date in USD [D]. Bank credit to the sector is up 23.3% YoY against that output fall — a 28.9 pp gap [D]. So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower is funding a stock build with borrowed money; if inventory days are rising while sales fall, ask why the drawing power is still being renewed.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue branded and mid-premium converters with export diversification.** Peer results show the split: Lux grew revenue 13% with 17% volume growth and export revenue up 52% into GCC and Africa [5]; Rupa grew 10.4% YoY in Q1 FY27 [7]; Dollar posted 22.1% YoY growth [7]. Rupa's Q4 FY26 EBITDA margin was 12.5% on 9% volume growth, with 4-5% price increases taken [4]. **Avoid pure wholesale winterwear converters selling only into North India** — they carry the full raw-material shock with no pricing power. Note the Crisil 10-12% growth call is from December 2024 [9][11] and is now stale.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle, not the fixed assets.** Take monthly stock and debtor statements, and a monthly dyeing-job-work register to confirm throughput. Cap drawing power at a realistic inventory-and-receivables base; if the borrower cannot produce the register, ask for the job-work bills. ICRA's textile methodology flags the sector as fixed- and working-capital intensive with high funding needs [10]. Punjab received just 0.3% of the Centre's textile skilling funds [3], so do not underwrite on promised subsidies. Local dyeing units are running on paddy straw amid fuel shortages [1] — treat energy continuity as a live risk, not a footnote.

## Early-warning signs
- **Monthly stock statement (monthly):** inventory days rising while sales fall -> freeze enhancement, re-price.
- **GST returns vs bank turnover (monthly):** gap widening -> ask for buyer-wise sales ledger.
- **Raw-material cost pass-through (quarterly):** price hikes not sticking -> shift to secured, shorter-tenor limits.
- **Export order book (quarterly):** GCC/Africa orders thinning -> reduce limit.
